exercises.title: Accessibility Advocacy Language
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - Master the vocabulary for making the business case for accessibility: ROI arguments, legal risk, roadmap framing, and responding to stakeholder objections.

questions.q: A product manager asks: "Why should we prioritise accessibility now? Our analytics don't show many disabled users." Which response is the most effective business case argument?
options: Because analytics under-count disabled users (many use workarounds), the addressable market is much larger than it appears - 1 in 5 people globally have a disability, accessibility improvements benefit all users, and retrofitting later costs 5-10× more than building in from the start.
Because it is the right thing to do ethically.
Because our competitors are doing it.
Because disabled users will sue if we don't comply.
questions.explanation: Effective accessibility advocacy combines three business arguments: 1. Market size (the analytics problem): • ~1.3 billion people globally have some form of disability (WHO) • Analytics under-count them - users with assistive technologies often block JavaScript, skew session data • The "disability" label misses situational disability: someone using the app one-handed while commuting 2. Total user benefit (the curb-cut effect): • Captions benefit: deaf users + non-native speakers + noisy environments + silent commuters • High contrast benefits: users with low vision + people in bright sunlight • Keyboard navigation benefits: power users, developers, enterprise users 3. Cost of retrofitting: • Research shows post-launch accessibility fixes cost 5-10× more than building in during design • Every sprint that ships inaccessible features adds to the debt Key vocabulary: • addressable market - the total potential customers for a product • curb-cut effect - accessibility features that benefit a broader population than originally intended • retrofit - adding accessibility to existing code after the fact • analytics under-counting - when tracking tools miss segments of users who use workarounds

questions.q: A legal team asks you to explain the difference between ADA , WCAG , and EAA . Which explanation is correct?
options: All three are voluntary guidelines - none create legal liability.
ADA is a design guideline; WCAG is a law; EAA is a testing framework.

ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) is US civil rights law; WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the technical standard published by W3C that defines what "accessible" means; EAA (European Accessibility Act) is EU law mandating WCAG conformance for products sold in the EU by 2025.
They are three names for the same US federal law requiring accessible websites.
questions.explanation: Understanding the legal landscape is essential for accessibility advocacy: ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) - 1990, US: • Civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against people with disabilities • Courts have repeatedly held that websites are "places of public accommodation" covered by the ADA • No specific technical standard mandated, but WCAG 2.1 AA is the de facto standard used in settlements • Thousands of ADA web accessibility lawsuits filed annually WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) - W3C: • Technical standard, not a law itself • Levels: A (minimum), AA (standard), AAA (enhanced) • WCAG 2.1 AA is the most widely required level in law and procurement • WCAG 2.2 published October 2023 with new criteria EAA (European Accessibility Act) - EU Directive 2019/882: • Became enforceable June 28, 2025 in EU member states • Requires WCAG conformance for digital products and services sold in the EU • Penalties vary by member state; significant fines possible Other laws to know: • Section 508 (US federal procurement), EN 301 549 (EU standard for public procurement), AODA (Canada/Ontario) Key vocabulary: • conformance - meeting all requirements of a standard (WCAG conformance) • AA (Double-A) - the intermediate WCAG conformance level required by most laws • procurement requirement - an accessibility condition that must be met for a product to be purchased by government

questions.q: An engineer pushes back: "Accessibility is a niche concern - our users are developers, they don't have disabilities." How do you respond most effectively?
options: Let's run a survey to find out how many of our users have disabilities.

Disabled developers exist and deserve equal access to developer tools - Twitter's developer portal, GitHub, and VS Code all invest in accessibility for exactly this reason. Additionally, keyboard-first navigation and screen reader support improve DX for all power users.
You're right, developer tools have different standards.
I understand, but we have to comply with the law.
questions.explanation: Countering the "our users don't have disabilities" myth requires facts and concrete examples: Reality check on developer disability rates: • The Stack Overflow Developer Survey consistently shows ~13-20% of developers report some form of disability • Developer tools (IDEs, dashboards, CLI tools, web portals) are used by people with visual, motor, and cognitive disabilities • Companies: Salesforce, Microsoft (VS Code), GitHub, GitLab all have dedicated accessibility programs for developer tools The power user argument: • Keyboard navigation = faster for all developers, not just those who need it • Screen reader-compatible tables = better semantic structure for all users • High-contrast themes = already a popular feature in every major IDE The inclusive team argument: • When you build inaccessible tools, you can't hire disabled developers (your users become your colleagues) • Cognitive accessibility (clear error messages, predictable navigation) reduces cognitive load for everyone under stress Key vocabulary: • DX (Developer Experience) - the overall experience of developers using a tool or platform • keyboard-first - design approach that ensures full functionality via keyboard before adding mouse interactions • cognitive load - the mental effort required to use a system; accessibility reduces cognitive load for all users

questions.q: A CFO asks: "What's the ROI on accessibility? Give me a number." Which response most effectively answers the question?
options: "Accessibility doesn't have a traditional ROI - it's about values."
"I can't give you a specific number without a full audit."

"Studies show that accessible sites have 35% higher revenue, though context varies. The more quantifiable cost is the legal risk: a single ADA lawsuit settlement typically costs $25,000-$250,000 plus attorney fees, plus remediation under court order. Preventing one lawsuit funds years of proactive accessibility work."
"All our competitors have done it so we should too."
questions.explanation: CFOs respond to numbers - accessibility advocacy must speak the language of risk and return: Quantifiable legal risk (most compelling for CFOs): • ADA Title III web accessibility lawsuits: 4,000+ filed in US in recent years • Average settlement: $25,000-$90,000 (small companies) to multi-million (large brands) • Court-ordered remediation: often requires external audit + redesign under monitoring • Repeat plaintiff risk: serial litigants file hundreds of cases - once flagged, you may face multiple suits Revenue argument: • Accessible e-commerce sites report higher conversion from users with disabilities • Click-Away Pound Report (UK): disabled users spend £420 billion annually; inaccessible sites lose this revenue • Forrester Research: accessible sites have lower bounce rates and higher overall usability scores Cost avoidance (proactive vs reactive): • IBM research: fixing a bug during design = $1; during testing = $15; post-release = $100 • Accessibility debt compounds just like technical debt Key vocabulary: • ROI (Return on Investment) - the financial return relative to the cost of an investment • remediation cost - the expense of fixing accessibility issues after they've been shipped • legal exposure - the potential financial liability from lawsuits or regulatory fines • proactive vs reactive - building in vs. fixing after the fact

questions.q: You are presenting an accessibility roadmap to leadership. Which framing is most likely to secure budget approval?
options: "Other companies have been sued, so we should be worried."

"Accessibility is a feature, not a bug fix - phased investment: (1) remediate P0 violations (legal risk reduction), (2) integrate into design system (prevents future debt), (3) certification-ready compliance audit - total cost X, avoids estimated lawsuit risk of Y per incident."
"Disabled users deserve equal access to our product."
"We need to fix all WCAG AA violations before we ship any new features."
questions.explanation: Roadmap framing that wins budget approval uses: phased approach, cost quantification, and risk comparison. Why "phased investment" framing works: • Leadership can approve a manageable Phase 1 without committing to full compliance upfront • Each phase shows measurable progress (fewer violations, design system integration) • Risk reduction provides justification even without revenue lift numbers Structure of a persuasive accessibility roadmap: 1. Current state audit: # WCAG AA violations, severity, affected flows 2. Legal risk quantification: probability × typical settlement cost 3. Phase 1 - P0 remediation: critical path violations; cost + timeline 4. Phase 2 - Design system integration: prevents future debt; shift-left 5. Phase 3 - Certification: VPAT, external audit, compliance statement Language patterns for leadership presentations: • "This investment reduces our legal exposure from X to Y" • "Remediating post-launch costs 5× more than integrating into the design system now" • "Phase 1 targets the flows most vulnerable to litigation: checkout, authentication, forms" Key vocabulary: • VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) - a document that describes how a product meets accessibility standards; often required for enterprise/government procurement • P0 violation - a critical accessibility barrier that prevents a user from completing a core task • shift-left - integrating accessibility (or any quality concern) earlier in the development process • compliance statement - a public declaration of a product's WCAG conformance level

Ensure label is a string and has a maximum length of 64 characters.", "details": { "field": "label", "reason": "invalid_value" } } ``` During a code review, your colleague points out this API response. You need to explain to the team why this specific error is significant from an accessibility perspective. Which comment best captures the issue?
options: 'The API is rejecting requests because the `label` field isn't properly formatted. This likely means screen readers aren't receiving descriptive text for form elements, which violates WCAG 1.4.1.'
'This is just a technical glitch; let's fix the backend.'

The API's rejection of the `label` field because it's missing or improperly formatted demonstrates a failure to provide accessible text for assistive technology users - specifically violating guideline 1.4.1 (Info and Relationships). Options B and C are too dismissive, while option D is a general statement without referencing accessibility standards. It's crucial to translate technical errors into their implications for user experience, particularly for those with disabilities.

questions.q: Sarah, a junior developer on your team, writes this PR description for a new form input field: ```html ``` During a code review, you notice the label associated with this input is missing. Which of the following responses would be most effective in communicating the importance of accessibility to Sarah?
options: D) 'Let's just leave it as is; it's simpler that way.'
C) 'The placeholder text is sufficient for accessibility; users don't need a separate label.'

B) 'Adding an explicit `aria-label` attribute or using the `for` attribute on the ` ` element is essential. This provides a screen reader with context and allows users who cannot see the placeholder text to understand the purpose of the field.'
A) 'Don't worry about it; users can still figure out what the field is for.'
questions.explanation: This question assesses the ability to advocate effectively with a less experienced developer. Option C provides the correct technical solution - using `aria-label` or the ` ` attribute - explaining *why* it's necessary for screen reader users. Options D and A are dismissive and ignore accessibility best practices. Option B is incorrect, as placeholder text isn't always sufficient, especially when visual cues aren't available.

questions.q: During a Slack conversation with the design team about a new UI component, Alex says: 'Just make it look good - accessibility is for lawyers.' Which response best communicates the importance of considering accessibility from a development perspective?
options: 'Actually, Alex, accessibility isn't about lawyers; it's fundamentally about providing an equal user experience for everyone, regardless of their abilities. It impacts our product's overall success.'
'Let's focus on making it visually appealing first, and then we can address any accessibility concerns if they arise.'
'I understand you want it to look good, but accessibility is just about following guidelines - we don't really need to worry about the underlying reasons.'

'That's a fair point, but focusing solely on aesthetics can lead to significant usability issues and potential legal challenges down the line. We need to proactively ensure our component meets established standards.'
questions.explanation: The correct answer emphasizes the core principle of equal user experience. The misconception is that accessibility is solely a legal matter or a task for specialists. Options C and B downplay the importance of inclusive design, while option A correctly frames it as a fundamental usability concern. Option D provides a more detailed explanation and justification.

questions.q: You're reviewing a code change that implements a new API endpoint. The documentation for the endpoint includes this JSON response: ```json { "status": "success", "data": { "userId": 123, "userName": "John Doe" } } ``` The API client is experiencing issues and reporting a '400 Bad Request' error. Which of the following best describes how you should communicate this issue to the backend team?
options: 'The API endpoint is returning a 400 error, which means the request was invalid. Please investigate the client-side code.'
'The response indicates success, but the client isn't receiving the expected data. There might be an issue with data serialization or mapping on the client side.'
'Let the QA team handle this; they're better equipped to diagnose issues with API responses.'
'The API documentation is incorrect; it should state that a 400 error indicates a problem with the request payload itself - likely missing required fields.'
questions.explanation: The correct response acknowledges that while the *status* field indicates success, the *data* is missing. This suggests a problem with data handling on the client side (serialization, mapping). Options A and C deflect responsibility or suggest inappropriate troubleshooting steps. Option D misinterprets the meaning of a 400 error - it's a general indication of an invalid request, not necessarily a specific field being missing.

exercises.title: 🔍 Accessibility Audit Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Master the language of accessibility audits: findings, severity, VPAT, and remediation vocabulary. Intermediate

questions.q: The audit report cites WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.7 - Focus Visible . What does a success criterion citation in an accessibility audit mean?
options: The finding traces the violation to a specific WCAG requirement - allowing developers to understand the normative standard that was not met and what needs to be fixed.
The audit was conducted using automated tools only.
The issue was found manually by a disabled user tester.
The issue is a best practice recommendation, not a normative requirement.
questions.explanation: Each WCAG success criterion citation in an audit report gives the finding a traceable, normative reference: Citation component Example Purpose SC number 2.4.7 Unique identifier - enables lookup SC name Focus Visible Human-readable label Level AA Indicates compliance priority Citing the SC separates normative violations (must fix for legal compliance) from best-practice recommendations (should fix). Key vocabulary: "success criterion reference" , "normative requirement" , "understanding SC" , "sufficient technique" .

questions.q: The automated scan found 12 violations using axe-core . What is the key limitation of automated accessibility testing?
options: Automated tools require a paid license for production testing.
Automated tools cannot test single-page applications.
Automated tools only work with WCAG 1.0 criteria.
Automated tools (like axe-core) can find around 30-40% of WCAG violations - the rest require human judgment and assistive technology testing.
questions.explanation: Automated accessibility tools are fast and consistent but cover only a portion of WCAG requirements: Testing type Finds Misses Automated (axe-core) Missing alt text, contrast failures, missing labels, duplicate IDs Wrong alt text, cognitive accessibility, keyboard flow quality Manual review Context-dependent issues, logical structure, reading order Comprehensive AT experience AT testing Screen reader comprehension, forms mode, focus management Efficiency - requires AT expertise Key vocabulary: "automated + manual testing requirement" , "false negative" , "automated audit coverage (30-40%)" , "expert review" .

questions.q: The audit finding has severity: Critical . What does severity in an accessibility audit typically mean?
options: How difficult the issue is to fix technically.
The legal penalty for not fixing the issue.
How many users are affected by the issue.

The degree of impact on disabled users - Critical = completely blocks access for a user group (e.g., unlabelled form fields, keyboard trap); Major = significantly impairs use; Minor = causes friction but user can work around it.
questions.explanation: Severity classification helps teams prioritise remediation regardless of WCAG level: Severity User impact Example Critical Access completely blocked for a user group Keyboard trap, form with no labels Major Significantly impairs but does not block Poor focus management in modal Minor Friction - user can work around it Heading level skipped in one section Severity is independent of WCAG level - a Level A issue can be Minor in context; a Level AA issue can be Critical if it blocks screen reader users. Key vocabulary: "access blocker" , "remediation priority" , "user impact vs. WCAG level" .

questions.q: The VPAT shows "Supports with Exceptions" for SC 1.4.11. What does "Supports with Exceptions" in a VPAT mean?
options: The product generally meets the criterion but has specific components or instances that do not conform - partially accessible with known gaps.
The product has been granted an exception from this requirement by a regulatory body.
The product fully meets the success criterion.
The criterion does not apply to this product category.
questions.explanation: VPAT conformance level designations communicate the product's accessibility status for each success criterion: VPAT designation Meaning Supports Fully meets the success criterion Partially Supports / Supports with Exceptions Some components do not conform; known gaps documented in notes Does Not Support The criterion is not met Not Applicable The criterion does not apply to this product type Key vocabulary: "VPAT conformance claim" , "exception documentation" , "remediation roadmap in VPAT notes" , "honest self-assessment" .

questions.q: The remediation recommendation is to add a visible focus indicator to all interactive elements. What SC does this recommendation address and why is it important?
options: SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships - keyboard focus conveys semantic information.
SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value - focus state must be communicated to assistive technology.
SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA) / SC 2.4.11 Focus Appearance Enhanced (AA in WCAG 2.2) - keyboard users need to see which element has focus to navigate the page.
SC 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum - focus rectangles must meet contrast thresholds.
questions.explanation: Focus visible requirements ensure sighted keyboard users can navigate without a mouse: Criterion Requirement WCAG version SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible Any keyboard-operable UI must have a visible focus indicator 2.1 - Level AA SC 2.4.11 Focus Appearance Stricter: focus indicator must have minimum area and contrast 2.2 - Level AA outline: none in CSS = accessibility failure. Key vocabulary: "focus indicator" , "focus ring" , "outline: none anti-pattern" , "keyboard navigation baseline" , "focus management in SPAs" .

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I've just run the accessibility audit on the new payment API. Axe-core flagged 37 violations related to insufficient color contrast in the form fields and missing ARIA labels for several buttons. Should we prioritize fixing these based on the report?"
options: The number of violations (37) itself suggests a high priority, but we should investigate the specific types to determine impact.
Insufficient color contrast is a low-priority issue, as long as the user can still complete the payment.
Prioritize fixing all 37 violations immediately; the audit report indicates critical accessibility issues.
Color contrast is less important than missing ARIA labels. Let's focus on those first.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights a common situation in code reviews . While all violations deserve attention, the report's designation of 'critical' issues - like insufficient color contrast - often represents a significant barrier for users with visual impairments. Prioritizing these high-severity items ensures immediate improvements to core functionality and demonstrates commitment to accessibility best practices. Focusing solely on ARIA labels without addressing contrast could still lead to usability problems, so a balanced approach is key.

questions.q: PR Description: 'Implemented minor styling changes to the user interface. Added some padding and adjusted font sizes for better readability.' Reviewer Alex comments: 'This looks good, but have you considered running an accessibility audit? Specifically, are you ensuring sufficient color contrast between text and background elements according to WCAG guidelines?'
options: Alex is pointing out that the styling changes may violate WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) if the adjusted font sizes or padding result in insufficient contrast for users with low vision.
Alex is questioning the user interface's overall aesthetic appeal, suggesting a more modern design style.
Alex is suggesting a general UI improvement. Ensuring sufficient color contrast is a separate design consideration unrelated to accessibility.
Alex is concerned about potential SEO issues related to the styling changes.
questions.explanation: Alex's comment highlights the critical connection between UI styling and accessibility. WCAG 1.4.3 specifically addresses sufficient color contrast as a requirement for readability - failing to meet this criterion can make content inaccessible to users with low vision. The PR description focuses solely on aesthetic changes without considering their impact on user experience and, crucially, adherence to accessibility standards. This demonstrates the importance of proactively incorporating accessibility considerations during development.

questions.q: During a code review for a new e-commerce checkout flow, Developer Ben notes in the comment: 'I've run an automated accessibility scan using Lighthouse. It highlighted several issues related to keyboard navigation - specifically, missing `tabindex` attributes on some interactive elements and inconsistent focus order.' What is Ben primarily referring to when discussing these Lighthouse findings?
options: insufficient - the checkout process lacks a clear visual indication of progress.
a high number of visual contrast violations across all elements of the page.
duplicate form fields causing confusion and errors during data entry.
poor keyboard navigation - the scan identified issues with how users can navigate the flow using a keyboard, hindering accessibility for those who cannot use a mouse.
questions.explanation: Ben is focusing on 'keyboard navigation' which relates to WCAG success criterion 2.1.2 No Keyboard Input Component Removed. The scan identified problems with how users navigate a website using only the keyboard, such as missing `tabindex` attributes or an inconsistent focus order, directly impacting those who rely on keyboards for interaction - a key accessibility consideration. These issues often cause significant difficulty for users with motor impairments.

questions.q: Alex , the lead developer on the project, sends this Slack message to the team: 'Just finished a quick accessibility audit of the new admin dashboard. Axe-core reported 23 violations primarily relating to low color contrast and missing alternative text for images. Should we focus our immediate efforts on addressing these findings, or are there other issues we should prioritize based on the severity?' What is Alex most concerned about when requesting this review?
options: The number of violations reported by Axe-core indicates that the dashboard likely has significant accessibility issues, but further investigation is needed to determine their severity and impact.
Missing alternative text for images always represents a critical accessibility failure requiring immediate attention.
Low color contrast is a non-issue as long as it's within a reasonable range.
Axe-core's findings are irrelevant because Alex personally tested the dashboard and found no accessibility problems.
questions.explanation: Alex is rightly concerned about the high number of violations reported by Axe-core. While low color contrast can be a factor, multiple violations point to a systemic issue requiring immediate attention. The key takeaway here is that automated scans like Axe-core often highlight areas needing focused investigation - it's not simply about resolving every single flagged item immediately but understanding the overall accessibility status and prioritizing based on severity. The other options misinterpret the role of automated testing or assume low color contrast automatically represents a critical failure.

questions.q: During a standup update, David says: 'We've just completed an accessibility audit of the new data visualization tool using Lighthouse. The scan identified several issues related to screen reader compatibility - specifically, missing or poorly implemented `aria-*` attributes on charts and graphs, and insufficient semantic HTML.' What is David primarily raising concern about in this statement?
options: Missing alternative text descriptions for images.
Insufficient color contrast impacting visual impairments.
Lack of keyboard navigation support for users with motor disabilities.
Poorly structured code that violates WCAG guidelines.
questions.explanation: David is highlighting the lack of keyboard navigation support, which directly relates to screen reader accessibility. The `aria-*` attributes and semantic HTML are often used to provide assistive technologies with information needed to interpret and interact with complex UI elements like charts and graphs. A failure in these areas significantly impacts users who rely on screen readers for access.

questions.q: A developer says 'I tested with NVDA'. What is NVDA?
options: A browser developer tools panel
A free, open-source screen reader for Windows
A colour contrast checking extension
An automated accessibility linting rule set

questions.q: What does 'keyboard-only navigation testing' involve?
options: Testing the site using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Escape, and arrow keys without a mouse
Running an automated keyboard shortcut audit
Verifying that all keyboard shortcuts are documented
Checking that the site has no keyboard shortcuts
questions.explanation: Keyboard-only testing means navigating the entire interface using only the keyboard to verify all interactive elements are reachable, operable, and have a visible focus indicator.

questions.q: A QA engineer says 'the axe scan found 3 violations'. What is axe?
options: A manual screen reader test protocol
An automated accessibility testing engine that identifies WCAG violations in HTML
A colour-blindness simulation tool
A keyboard navigation recorder
questions.explanation: axe (by Deque) is a widely used automated accessibility testing engine available as a browser extension, CLI tool, and testing library integration that flags WCAG violations.

questions.q: When a tester says 'this fails the accessibility audit in Lighthouse', what does that mean?
options: The page load time is too slow
Chrome's Lighthouse tool detected accessibility issues such as missing alt text or low contrast
The page is blocked by a robots.txt rule
The site has JavaScript errors
questions.explanation: Lighthouse is a Chrome tool that runs automated audits including accessibility checks. An accessibility audit failure means the page has detectable WCAG issues such as missing labels, poor contrast, or inaccessible forms.

questions.q: What is 'VoiceOver' in the context of accessibility testing?
options: A browser plugin for audio testing
The built-in screen reader on Apple macOS and iOS
A speech synthesis API in JavaScript
A screen recording tool for creating tutorials
questions.explanation: VoiceOver is the built-in screen reader on Apple devices (macOS, iOS, iPadOS) and is essential for testing accessibility on Apple platforms alongside NVDA/JAWS on Windows.

questions.q: Sarah : 'Hey team, I ran a contrast check on the primary button using WebAIM's Contrast Checker. The results show it's significantly below WCAG AA standards - we need to address this immediately!'. What does 'WCAG' stand for in this context?

World Wide Computer Architecture Group
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
Windows Client Application Gateway

VoiceOver automatically adjusts its reading speed based on the complexity of the page, ensuring all elements are thoroughly covered during testing.
questions.explanation: This question focuses on a crucial aspect of screen reader testing beyond just visual element highlighting. Verify that the form elements are consistently announced by VoiceOver and that keyboard navigation is functional.
Insufficient - the account balance is too low...
Confirm that the primary button has a sufficient color contrast ratio for users with low vision.

Focus solely on ensuring basic accessibility functionality, as Lighthouse is too complex for a quick review.

exercises.title: Accessible Forms & ARIA Live Regions
exercises.subtitle: Learn the IT-English vocabulary for building accessible forms: labels, error association, fieldsets and aria-live announcements.

questions.q: A developer says: 'Wrap the radio buttons in a fieldset with a legend.' What does the 'legend' provide?
options: A colour key for the form
A group label describing the set of related controls
A loading spinner
A submit handler
questions.explanation: A gives an accessible group label so screen readers announce the purpose of the grouped controls.

questions.q: An aria-live region is set to 'polite'. What does 'polite' mean?
options: The update is announced immediately, interrupting the user
The update is announced when the screen reader finishes its current speech
The region is hidden visually
The region cannot be edited
questions.explanation: aria-live='polite' queues the announcement until the screen reader is idle, rather than interrupting.

questions.q: What does it mean to 'associate' an error message with its input?
options: To place it nearby visually only
To programmatically link them with aria-describedby so the reader announces the error when the field is focused
To log the error to the console
To colour the field red
questions.explanation: Associating via aria-describedby links the error text to the field so assistive tech announces it.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'accessible name'?
options: The accessible name is the input's background colour.
The label provides the input's accessible name, which the screen reader announces.
The accessible name is the form's URL.
The accessible name is set with CSS.
questions.explanation: The accessible name is the text assistive tech uses to identify a control - usually from its label.

questions.q: A spec says required fields should not rely on colour alone. Why?
options: Colour is hard to render
Users with colour blindness or screen readers won't perceive the requirement; use text or aria-required too
Colours slow the page
Colour breaks validation
questions.explanation: Indicating requirement only by colour fails accessibility; add a text marker and aria-required.

questions.q: During a code review of a new form component for user registration, Sarah points out that the `aria-live='off'` attribute is used on a section displaying real-time validation feedback. Mark replies: 'But the users need to *know* immediately when their email address isn't valid!' What is the most appropriate response you should give Mark? Options: A : ' aria-live='off' is correct because it prevents unnecessary screen reader announcements. The user can always check the form for errors later.' B : 'That's fine; users will just see the error message when they submit the form, which is standard practice.' C : 'We should use aria-live='polite' instead. This ensures that the announcement happens after the user has finished interacting with the form, minimizing disruption.' D : 'The section doesn't *need* aria-live at all. We should just style the error message differently.'
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: Mark is focused on immediate feedback, but using aria-live='off' effectively disables any real-time announcements. While styling the error message is important, aria-live provides a direct mechanism to alert screen reader users *immediately* of input errors - this is crucial for accessibility. Using aria-live='polite' would be more appropriate for a less critical update, but 'off' completely prevents the announcement, which isn't accessible.

questions.q: During a Slack conversation about implementing real-time validation for a new e-commerce form, David proposes using aria-live='off' on a section that displays immediate feedback when an input field has an error. Maria replies: 'But we need to immediately alert the user when they enter an invalid credit card number!' What is the primary reason why using aria-live='off' in this scenario might be problematic, and what alternative approach would likely be more appropriate for ensuring accessibility compliance?
options: A: 'aria-live='off' is optimal because it prevents excessive screen reader notifications. Users can review the form's validation status at their convenience.'

B: 'Using aria-live='off' here allows the section to remain hidden until a deliberate user action, such as focusing on the input field. This approach aligns with best practices for managing screen reader announcements.'
C: ' aria-live='polite' is the correct choice; it ensures the announcement happens after the user has finished interacting with the form, minimizing disruption and respecting their workflow.'
D: 'The section should be styled differently to highlight errors. Using aria-live is unnecessary for providing immediate feedback to users'
questions.explanation: The problem lies in aria-live='off' effectively disables the screen reader from announcing any updates to the section. While it prevents *unnecessary* announcements, it also prevents the user from receiving critical validation information when they need it most - namely, when entering an invalid credit card number. aria-live='polite' is significantly more appropriate because it allows the announcement to occur after the user has interacted with the form (e.g., focused on the input field), ensuring the user receives timely feedback without disrupting their flow.

questions.q: During a code review of a new form component for user registration, Alex comments: 'I've added aria-live='off' to the section displaying real-time validation feedback. It prevents screen readers from constantly announcing errors while the user is typing.' Ben replies: 'But what about users who might have low vision and rely heavily on screen reader announcements?' What is the most critical concern with Alex's approach, and what should he consider to ensure a truly accessible experience for all users?
options: A: aria-live='off' is perfectly acceptable; Ben is overreacting. The user can always revisit the form after submitting it to check for errors.

B: Alex is correct in minimizing screen reader announcements, but he should also consider providing a visual indicator of validation status alongside the screen reader feedback - perhaps using a subtle icon change or a brief message displayed on hover.
C: aria-live='off' is incorrect; it actively prevents assistive technologies from functioning as intended. The form should always announce errors immediately.
D: Alex's approach is fine, and Ben's concern about low vision users is not relevant to the core accessibility requirements for this form.
questions.explanation: Alex's use of aria-live='off' creates a significant accessibility barrier. While minimizing announcements can be beneficial in some contexts, it prevents screen reader users from receiving immediate feedback on invalid input - a crucial element for usability and error correction. Ben's concern about low vision users highlights the importance of providing redundant information channels, like a visual indicator alongside the screen reader announcement, to cater to diverse user needs and ensure full accessibility.

questions.q: What does the ARIA attribute `role="navigation"` communicate to assistive technologies?

polite works in Safari only; assertive works cross-browser
questions.explanation: aria-live="polite" announces updates after the user finishes their current action; aria-live="assertive" interrupts immediately and should be used only for critical alerts.

options: The button is disabled
The controlled content is currently collapsed/hidden
The button has not been clicked yet
The button is outside the viewport

When the label must be translated automatically

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm updating the API response for the user profile. I've added an aria-describedby attribute to the element that contains the address details. Is this correct?"

correct - aria-describedby links the element to a label text for screen readers.

incorrect - aria-describedby is only suitable for complex, multi-part descriptions; use aria-details instead.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the purpose of aria-describedby : it establishes a link between an element and another source of information (in this case, the label text within the details section) for screen reader users. The common misconception is to think of aria-describedby as simply providing a basic description; it's designed to connect to existing labels or other elements that offer more context. Using aria-label would be an alternative approach but less precise in this scenario.

questions.q: David : "I'm submitting this PR to update the dashboard layout. I've used aria-label on the 'Refresh Data' button to provide a text description for screen readers. Should I be using aria-describedby instead?"
options: insufficient - the button should always have a visible label.

This creates a stronger semantic connection for assistive technologies and clarifies the purpose of the button more effectively. Using aria-describedby allows you to precisely control which element provides the description, unlike aria-label which relies on the label being present on the button itself.

questions.q: Mark comments on a PR: "Just noticed this button isn't accessible. It lacks a clear label and doesn't use any ARIA attributes to describe its function. Users with screen readers won't know what it does.". Which of the following approaches would Mark recommend to improve accessibility in this situation?
options: Add aria-label="Submit Form" to the button element, clearly describing its purpose. Also consider adding aria-describedby to link to a more detailed description if needed.
The PR should be rejected immediately; accessibility is paramount and requires a complete overhaul of the UI before deployment.
questions.explanation: Mark's suggestion correctly identifies the two key components for accessible buttons: `aria-label` provides immediate context to screen readers, while `aria-describedby` allows linking to more detailed information if needed. The other options either misinterpret the role of each attribute or offer overly simplistic (and ultimately insufficient) solutions. It's crucial that developers understand the difference between providing a concise label and offering supplementary descriptive content for assistive technology users.

questions.q: John : "I'm reviewing this PR. The component uses aria-hidden="true" on the loading spinner. Should I remove it? It seems like a visual indicator is enough."
options: insufficient - the user needs to know the component is loading, regardless of visibility.
correct - hiding the spinner prevents visual clutter and doesn't negatively impact usability.

The correct approach is to provide alternative descriptive text using aria-live or a properly labeled button, ensuring all users have access to the same information.

questions.q: The developer is testing with NVDA + Firefox . What type of assistive technology is NVDA?
options: A keyboard remapping utility for motor-impaired users.
A browser-based contrast checker.
A screen magnification tool.
A screen reader - software that reads page content and announces it to blind or low-vision users via synthesised speech or a Braille display.
questions.explanation: NVDA (NonVisual Desktop Access) is a free, open-source Windows screen reader. Screen readers are among the most widely used assistive technologies: Screen reader Platform Best paired browser NVDA Windows (free) Firefox / Chrome JAWS Windows (enterprise) Chrome / Firefox VoiceOver macOS / iOS (built-in) Safari TalkBack Android (built-in) Chrome Key vocabulary: "screen reader" , "speech output" , "Braille display" , "browse mode vs. forms mode" , "virtual buffer" .

questions.q: An accessibility test plan includes "keyboard-only navigation testing" . What does this mean?
options: Testing the application using only the keyboard shortcut commands.
Testing that all keyboard shortcuts work without a mouse.
Verifying that no keyboard shortcuts conflict with screen reader shortcuts.
Testing every task flow without using a mouse - using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrow keys, and Escape - ensuring all features are reachable and operable with keyboard alone.
questions.explanation: Keyboard-only testing validates SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A) - all functionality must be operable without a mouse: Key Action Tab Move focus to the next interactive element Shift+Tab Move focus to the previous interactive element Enter / Space Activate focused button or control Arrow keys Navigate within widgets (menus, radios, tabs) Escape Close modals, dismissing overlays Common fails: focus traps, mouse-only event handlers ( onmouseover with no keyboard equivalent), invisible focus. Key vocabulary: "Tab order" , "keyboard trap" , "focus management" , "keyboard operability (SC 2.1.1)" .

questions.q: The video has captions but no audio description . What is the difference between captions and audio description?
options: Captions appear below the video; audio description appears above.
Audio description is just a louder version of the existing audio track.
Captions = text synchronised to speech and sounds (for Deaf/hard-of-hearing users); audio description = narrated description of visual content (for blind/low-vision users).
Captions are optional; audio description is legally required.
questions.explanation: Captions and audio descriptions serve different disability groups and are governed by separate WCAG success criteria: Feature Serves WCAG criterion Captions Deaf / hard-of-hearing users SC 1.2.2 - Level A Audio description Blind / low-vision users SC 1.2.5 - Level AA Captions ≠ subtitles: captions include non-speech audio cues (e.g., "[door slams]", "[music playing]"). Audio description narrates visual content not conveyed by existing audio. Key vocabulary: "closed vs. open captions" , "SDH (Subtitles for Deaf and Hard-of-hearing)" , "extended audio description" .

questions.q: The mobile app should be tested with an increased text size setting. Which disability does large text accommodation primarily support?
options: Motor impairment - large text makes touch targets easier to see.
Deaf users who rely on visual information.
Low vision - users who need enlarged text to read but do not use screen readers.
Colour blindness.
questions.explanation: Low vision users need enlarged content but typically interact visually - they are not the same as blind screen reader users: User Primary tool WCAG criterion Blind Screen reader (NVDA, JAWS) SC 1.3.1, 4.1.2 etc. Low vision Screen magnification, large text, high contrast SC 1.4.4 Text Resize (200%) SC 1.4.4: text must resize up to 200% without loss of content or functionality. Use relative font units ( rem / em ) not px . Key vocabulary: "low vision" , "Dynamic Type (iOS)" , "text resize (200%)" , "relative font units" , "zoom vs. text resize" .

options: Access keys only work in Internet Explorer.
Access keys slow down keyboard navigation by requiring extra key combinations.
Access keys conflict with screen reader shortcuts, OS shortcuts, and browser shortcuts - making them unreliable and potentially harmful to keyboard and assistive technology users.
Access keys require JavaScript to function.

questions.q: John and Maria are discussing a new web component that provides dynamic updates to user profiles. John notes that the component uses `MutationObserver` to track changes. questions.q: Microsoft's Inclusive Design framework describes "permanent, temporary, and situational" disability . How does this model change how teams approach accessibility?
options: It separates technical accessibility from inclusive design as different disciplines.
It provides a legal framework for ADA exemptions.
It classifies users into three groups that need separate designs.

It demonstrates that solutions designed for people with permanent disabilities benefit a far wider population - a permanently one-armed person, someone holding a baby, and someone with a broken arm all share the same constraint situation.
questions.explanation: The persona spectrum model expands who benefits from accessibility features: Disability type One arm example Permanent Born with one arm Temporary Arm in a cast after injury Situational Holding a baby, carrying shopping Curb cut effect: features designed for permanent disabilities benefit far more poeple - curb cuts designed for wheelchair users also help cyclists, parents with strollers, and delivery workers. Key vocabulary: "persona spectrum" , "curb cut effect" , "situational disability" , "design for the margins benefits the mainstream" .

questions.q: "We should design for the margins, not the average user." What does this principle mean in product design?
options: Designing for users with the most extreme constraints (disability, poor connectivity, cognitive differences) often produces better design for everyone - edge cases reveal design assumptions.
Design systems should use margins large enough for disabled users to avoid misclicks.
Products should target niche markets rather than mass-market audiences.
Designers should avoid average user research and focus only on disabled users.
questions.explanation: "Design for the margins" (Kat Holmes, Mismatch ) - excluding people reveals design rigidity: Edge case user What their constraint reveals Who else benefits Low-bandwidth user Unnecessary payload, slow render All users on slow connections Elderly / low digital literacy Confusing UX patterns Users in stressful contexts Non-native speaker Unclear copy and microcopy All users unfamiliar with UI Key vocabulary: "design justice" , "exclusion mapping" , "mismatch (Kat Holmes)" , "constraint-driven innovation" .

questions.q: The team is discussing cognitive accessibility for users with ADHD and dyslexia. Which of the following design choices most directly supports cognitive accessibility?
options: Ensuring all functionality is keyboard-accessible.
Providing audio descriptions for all visual content.
Using high-contrast colour combinations for all text.
Using plain language, consistent navigation, clear error messages, chunked content, and adequate time limits - reducing cognitive load for users with attention or reading differences.
questions.explanation: Cognitive accessibility addresses a different set of user needs from sensory or motor accessibility: Technique Helps with Plain language Reading differences (dyslexia), non-native speakers Consistent navigation Memory-related conditions, ADHD Clear error messages with recovery steps Reduces anxiety, supports all users Chunked content + visible progress ADHD, fatigue, cognitive overload No time pressure Processing speed differences Key vocabulary: "cognitive load" , "plain language" , "clear error recovery" , "SC 2.5.8 Target Size" , "COGA supplemental guidance" .

questions.q: An engineer says: "We'll add accessibility later once the feature is stable." Why is retrofitting accessibility after launch typically more expensive than building it in?
options: Retrofitting requires redesigning component architecture, DOM structure, and interaction patterns that were built without accessibility in mind - often requiring rework of multiple system layers rather than incremental additions.
Late accessibility work requires external consultants instead of internal engineers.
Accessibility tools cost more to license after product launch.
Legal penalties apply to every day the product is inaccessible before retrofitting.
questions.explanation: Shift-left accessibility - fixing accessibility issues earlier is dramatically cheaper: Phase Relative cost What needs changing Design 1× Spec update - add accessible name, keyboard behaviour Development 5× Code changes during active work - manageable After launch 20× Structural rework of component tree, DOM, interaction model If a component tree was built with div-based interactions, retrofitting ARIA and keyboard handling requires structural changes. Key vocabulary: "accessibility debt" , "shift-left accessibility" , "component API contract for accessibility" , "retrofit cost" .

questions.q: The design system team is building an accessible-by-default component library . What does "accessible by default" mean for a component library?
options: The library only uses native HTML elements, no custom components.
All components are styled with WCAG AA colour contrast by default.

Components are built with correct semantics, ARIA patterns, keyboard interactions, and focus management built in - reducing the work individual feature teams must do to achieve accessible implementations.
Developers using the library don't need to test for accessibility.
questions.explanation: An accessible-by-default component library encapsulates accessibility complexity so feature teams don't have to re-implement it: Component Built-in accessibility <Button /> Correct role, keyboard activation, focus ring, disabled state <Modal /> ARIA dialog pattern, focus trap on open, Escape to close, returns focus on close <Select /> Listbox pattern, arrow key navigation, type-ahead search Benefits: accessibility at scale, reduced individual team expertise requirement, consistent screen reader experience. Key vocabulary: "WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices" , "design system accessibility contract" , "accessibility token" .

questions.q: Reviewer: 'The button's color contrast isn't ideal. Users with low vision might struggle to see it.' You (as the UI designer) respond in a Slack message to the reviewer: 'Got it. I'll adjust the color palette and check the WCAG compliance levels for that button.' Which of the following best describes the core issue being raised, and your response's focus?
options: Insufficient - the button's contrast ratio violates accessibility guidelines, specifically regarding color perception for users with visual impairments.
Insufficient - the button's color is simply not visually appealing and requires a redesign.
Insufficient - the issue is related to the overall UI design, not just one element.
Insufficient - the Slack message focuses on technical details rather than user needs.
questions.explanation: The reviewer correctly identifies that the button's color contrast ratio falls short of accessibility standards (WCAG). This isn't simply about aesthetics; it addresses a core barrier for users with visual impairments. Your response demonstrates an understanding of this specific issue and a proactive step toward remediation - focusing on WCAG compliance is key to ensuring usability for everyone. The other options misinterpret the problem, suggesting aesthetic concerns or a broader UI redesign without addressing the fundamental accessibility gap.

questions.q: Sarah, a senior developer, is drafting a PR description for a new data visualization component. She writes: 'This chart displays sales figures - it's pretty and easy to understand!' Which of the following best describes the potential issue with Sarah's statement, and what should she add to improve accessibility?
options: The visualization lacks alternative text descriptions for screen reader users, failing to convey the information to visually impaired individuals.
The chart uses overly complex terminology that confuses non-technical users.
The chart doesn't provide sufficient data points for accurate analysis.
The code is poorly documented, making it difficult for developers to maintain.
questions.explanation: Sarah's statement prioritizes aesthetics and perceived ease of understanding over accessibility. A crucial element of accessible design is providing alternative text descriptions ( alt attributes) for all visual elements, including charts, so screen readers can convey the information to users who are visually impaired. Simply stating it's 'pretty and easy to understand' doesn't address the needs of diverse users.

questions.q: Mark, a junior developer, is discussing accessibility with his team during a standup meeting. He says: 'We should focus on making this feature accessible *after* we've finished building it.' Which of the following best explains why this approach is typically less effective and more costly?
options: Accessibility considerations are inherently subjective and require lengthy user testing after launch.
Developers prioritize features that are easiest to implement, which often neglects accessibility concerns.
Building accessibility in from the start (designing for inclusivity) is significantly faster than attempting to add it later due to the need to redesign existing code and workflows.
Retrofitting accessibility requires extensive re-architecting, leading to significant development time.
questions.explanation: Retrofitting accessibility after a feature is complete almost always involves substantial rework. It necessitates modifying existing code, potentially altering the application's architecture, and re-testing - all of which dramatically increase development time and cost compared to integrating accessibility considerations from the initial design phase.

exercises.title: Keyboard Navigation Patterns
exercises.subtitle: Master the IT-English vocabulary for keyboard accessibility: tab order, focus traps, skip links and roving tabindex.

questions.q: A reviewer writes: 'Please fix the tab order - it jumps around the page.' What does 'tab order' refer to?
options: The order of browser tabs
The sequence in which interactive elements receive focus when pressing Tab
The order of CSS classes
The order of imported modules
questions.explanation: Tab order is the sequence focus moves through interactive elements as the user presses Tab.

questions.q: What is a 'focus trap' in a modal dialog?
options: A bug where the page crashes
Keeping keyboard focus cycling within the open dialog until it is closed
A way to disable the keyboard
A logging mechanism
questions.explanation: A focus trap confines Tab navigation to the dialog so users can't tab into the hidden page behind it.

questions.q: A 'skip link' is added to the top of the page. What is its purpose?
options: To skip loading images
To let keyboard users jump straight to the main content, bypassing repeated navigation
To skip JavaScript execution
To redirect to another site
questions.explanation: A skip link lets keyboard and screen reader users bypass repetitive nav and jump to main content.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'roving tabindex'?
options: Use roving tabindex to make every menu item separately tabbable.
Use a roving tabindex so only one item in the list is in the tab order, and arrow keys move focus between items.
Roving tabindex disables the Tab key.
Roving tabindex is a CSS property.
questions.explanation: Roving tabindex keeps one item tabbable while arrow keys move active focus - a common composite-widget pattern.

questions.q: A bug says: 'The custom dropdown isn't operable by keyboard.' What does 'operable' mean here?
options: It can be styled
It can be fully used with the keyboard alone
It loads quickly
It is responsive on mobile
questions.explanation: 'Operable' (a WCAG principle) means users can interact with the control using the keyboard, not just a mouse.

questions.q: During a code review of the new admin panel, Sarah points out: 'I noticed that when I press Tab, it jumps unexpectedly between the 'Save' and 'Cancel' buttons. This makes it difficult to navigate the form consistently.' What is Sarah referring to when she mentions the 'Tab' key causing an unexpected jump in focus?
options: The browser's default scrolling behavior, which can interfere with keyboard navigation.
A problem with the CSS styling of the buttons, making them visually difficult to distinguish when focused.
Roving tabindex - the dynamic assignment of tab order based on element visibility, allowing for more flexible interaction patterns.
The user's mouse input overriding the Tab key's navigation function.
questions.explanation: Sarah is describing a situation where the tabindex attribute isn't being used correctly to control the order in which elements receive focus when the Tab key is pressed. It's not about scrolling or mouse input; it's specifically about the predictable sequence of keyboard interaction. The correct answer highlights that a CSS styling issue can cause unexpected behavior and hinder consistent navigation, even if tabindex is present.

questions.q: John in Slack: 'Just reviewed PR #123. The autocomplete field is *really* difficult to use with just the keyboard - it keeps jumping back to the input box instead of cycling through the suggestions.' What specific keyboard navigation pattern is John most likely describing?
options: A. A 'sticky' focus state.
B. A 'roving tabindex' issue.
C. An improperly configured 'auto-complete' widget with insufficient keyboard support.
D. A conflict between the tab order and the input field's event listeners.
questions.explanation: John is referring to a 'roving tabindex' problem. This happens when an element (like an autocomplete field) doesn't correctly update its `tabindex` value as you navigate through keyboard controls. It means the element isn't properly participating in the tab order, leading to unexpected focus jumps. Option A describes a different UI state; option C suggests a broader widget problem, while D is too general and doesn't directly address the observed behavior.

questions.q: During a sprint retrospective, David explains to the team that he's struggling with the new user onboarding flow. He says, 'I keep accidentally clicking the 'Submit' button because when I tab through the form fields, it briefly focuses on the button before I can move on. It's really frustrating!' What keyboard navigation pattern is David experiencing?
options: A: A focus trap - the user cannot escape the Submit button by pressing Escape or clicking outside of it.
B: Inconsistent tab order - the order in which elements receive focus changes unpredictably when using the Tab key.
C: Excessive tabindex values - the developer has inadvertently assigned very high `tabindex` values to form elements, causing rapid focus shifts.
D: A missing keyboard shortcut - there isn't a dedicated keyboard shortcut to submit the form, leading to accidental clicks.
questions.explanation: David is describing a focus trap , which occurs when the Tab key briefly focuses an element (in this case, the 'Submit' button) before returning focus to the previous field. This creates a jarring and disorienting experience for the user, as they are momentarily misplaced within the form. The core issue isn't a misconfiguration of `tabindex` or missing shortcuts; it's the uncontrolled shifting of focus that produces this trap-like behavior. Options C and D are not relevant to what he's describing.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a problem with the form. When I press Tab, it seems to 'bounce' back to the top of the field set before continuing. It's making it hard for users to clearly see what they are typing.' What is this behavior most likely related to regarding keyboard navigation?
options: Insufficient focus scope - the browser isn't correctly managing the tab order within the form.
Roving tabindex - the HTML attributes are causing unpredictable focus shifts.
Keyboard trapping - the element is preventing subsequent key presses from navigating out of it.
Unexpected focus ripple - the visual feedback after pressing Tab is not consistent with the actual tab target.
questions.explanation: This scenario describes a situation where the browser's default tab order isn't being properly maintained, causing the focus to jump back to the beginning of the form. The 'bounce' effect indicates that the Tab key is not reliably moving to the next interactive element in the intended sequence. Insufficient focus scope accurately captures this issue - the browser isn't correctly managing where keyboard focus is directed within the component.

questions.q: Alex in a Slack channel is discussing a UI component. He says: 'The keyboard navigation on this modal window is awful! When I press Tab, it just snaps back to the top of the dialog box every time - completely ignoring the rest of the controls.' What keyboard navigation issue is Alex describing?
options: Insufficient contrast between the focus indicator and the background.
A 'focus trap' where the modal window loses keyboard control entirely.
'Roving tabindex' causing unexpected jumps in focus within the modal's elements.
The use of a 'skip link' that is incorrectly implemented.
questions.explanation: Alex is describing a 'focus trap,' which happens when a keyboard user loses control over a UI element. This typically occurs due to an incorrect implementation of tabindex or focus management within the modal window itself; the Tab key isn't correctly cycling through all interactive elements. A roving tabindex issue would involve *intended* jumping, not accidental snapping back.

questions.q: What does the WCAG acronym POUR stand for?
options: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
Public, Open, Usable, Readable
Primary, Optional, Unique, Relevant
Programmatic, Observable, Uniform, Reliable
questions.explanation: POUR is the four-principle framework of WCAG: content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust for all users.

questions.q: A website is described as meeting 'WCAG 2.1 Level AA'. What does Level AA mean?
options: The site passes all possible accessibility checks
The site meets the middle conformance tier, covering the most widely required criteria
The site meets only the minimum baseline criteria
The site has passed an official government audit
questions.explanation: WCAG defines three conformance levels: A (minimum), AA (mid-level, most commonly required by laws and regulations), and AAA (highest/optional enhancements).

questions.q: A tester says 'the page fails success criterion 1.4.3'. What is success criterion 1.4.3 about?
options: Keyboard navigation
Contrast ratio between text and background
Audio description of video
Page language declaration
questions.explanation: SC 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum) requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text between foreground and background colours.

questions.q: Which WCAG principle covers the requirement that users must be able to navigate and use interface components with a keyboard?
options: Perceivable
Operable
Understandable
Robust
questions.explanation: The Operable principle (Principle 2) covers all interaction requirements, including keyboard accessibility (guideline 2.1) and sufficient time to interact (guideline 2.2).

questions.q: In a WCAG audit report, what does 'SC 4.1.2 - Name, Role, Value' test?
options: Whether text alternatives exist for images
Whether all UI components have accessible name, role, and state exposed to assistive technologies
Whether headings are in a logical order
Whether colour is not used as the only visual means of conveying information
questions.explanation: SC 4.1.2 requires that all user interface components have a name and role that can be programmatically determined, and states/values that can be set programmatically - critical for screen reader compatibility.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm reviewing this PR and noticed the form field labels aren't using ARIA roles. It seems like a Level A issue - we need to ensure screen reader users can understand what each field is for."
options: ARIA roles are only necessary for Level AAA compliance, so Sarah is overreacting.
Sarah is correctly identifying that missing ARIA roles violate WCAG 1.4.3 (Keyboard Accessible Name) and constitute a Level A non-compliance issue.
The PR's developer should simply add some descriptive text to the form fields; ARIA roles are unnecessary for basic accessibility.
Level A compliance is only about color contrast, so Sarah's concern is misplaced.
questions.explanation: Sarah correctly identifies a key WCAG guideline. Success Criterion 1.4.3 mandates that every operable UI component must have a name associated with it that is accessible to keyboard users. Missing ARIA roles effectively removes this name, making the form inaccessible for screen reader users and thus violating Level A standards. The other options misunderstand the scope of 1.4.3 or incorrectly associate it with color contrast.

questions.q: The WCAG 2.1 guidelines are organised around four principles - POUR . What does POUR stand for?
options: Portable, Open, Unified, Reachable - web platform principles.
Primary, Optional, Utility, Responsive - content priority framework.
Practical, Optimal, Usable, Responsive - the four dimensions of responsive design.
Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust - the four properties that all web content must have to be accessible.
questions.explanation: POUR describes the four foundational properties of accessible web content: Principle Meaning Perceivable Users can sense content with available senses (vision, hearing, touch) Operable Can interact regardless of input device (mouse, keyboard, switch) Understandable Content and UI behaviour makes sense to users Robust Works with current and future assistive technologies All 78 WCAG 2.1 success criteria map to one of these four principles. Key vocabulary: "WCAG principle" , "success criterion" , "conformance level (A/AA/AAA)" .

questions.q: The accessibility audit found a Level AA violation . What does WCAG Level AA conformance mean?
options: The page meets all Level A and Level AA success criteria - the standard required by most legal frameworks (EU EAA, US Section 508, UK PSBAR).
The page meets only the minimum legal accessibility baseline.
The page has been tested with a screen reader by a disabled user.
The page passes all possible WCAG success criteria.
questions.explanation: WCAG defines three conformance levels with increasing strictness: Level Criteria count Legal status A (minimum) 30 success criteria Baseline - rarely sufficient alone AA (standard) A + 20 additional Required by EU EAA, Section 508, UK PSBAR AAA (enhanced) AA + 28 additional Not achievable for all content types Key vocabulary: "conformance level" , "Level AA (standard requirement)" , "WCAG 2.2 adds 9 new criteria vs. 2.1" .

questions.q: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.3 requires a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text . What does this criterion address?
options: Colour choice restrictions for interfaces.
Sufficient contrast between text and background so people with low vision or colour blindness can read content.
